51
Supplement S3.6   Selection sort
S3.6 Selection sort: a stable extraction-and-shift variant
Change the movement, not just the tie test
Find the first minimum in the active suffix using strict <. Save that complete record. Shift
positions i through m-1 one place to the right, preserving their relative order, then put the saved
minimum at i. This removes the endpoint swap that caused instability.
STABLE-SELECTION(A)
  for i = 0 to length(A)-2
    m = i
    for j = i+1 to length(A)-1
      if key(A[j]) < key(A[m])
        m = j
    if m != i
      saved = A[m]
      for j = m downto i+1
        A[j] = A[j-1]
      A[i] = saved
Why equal records retain order
The first minimum precedes every other equal minimum still active. Placing it at the boundary
does not cross an earlier equal minimum. The shift moves every intervening record together and
does not reverse their mutual order. Repeating this reasoning establishes stable extraction for
every key group.
For (2,a), (2,b), (1,c), save c and shift a and b right. The result is (1,c), (2,a), (2,b), unlike the
ordinary-swap result. The globally-smallest-prefix proof for selection still applies, with
permutation preservation supplied by extraction plus shifting.
The tradeoff
Auxiliary storage remains O(1) records. The minimum searches still perform n(n-1)/2
comparisons. However, shifting can require Theta(n^2) array writes in the worst case. Thus the
ordinary selection sort's linear bound on nontrivial swaps does not translate into a linear
movement bound for this stable variant.

Supplement S3.7   Selection sort
S3.7 Selection sort: implementation, boundaries, and checks
In-place ordinary selection
The guard avoids self-swaps and makes the write convention explicit. This routine is correct for
comparable keys but does not promise stable tie order.
def selection_sort(a, key=lambda x: x):
    n = len(a)
    for i in range(n-1):
        m = i
        for j in range(i+1, n):
            if key(a[j]) < key(a[m]):
                m = j
        if m != i:
            a[i], a[m] = a[m], a[i]
    return a
Common failures
Reset m for each outer pass. Search only the unresolved suffix, including its final position. Do
not place a swap inside every candidate comparison and still describe the result as the one-swap
selection algorithm; that mutation is a different procedure with a different movement count.
The array can be empty: range(-1) produces no iterations in this Python listing. A singleton
similarly needs no pass. For descending order, update m when the candidate key is strictly
larger. For record sorting, exchange whole records and do not rewrite only their keys.
Checks that match the contract
For [5,1,4,2,8], expect [1,2,4,5,8], ten comparisons, and two guarded swaps. For labeled [ (2,a),
(2,b), (1,c) ], expect a numerically ordered output but do not assert stability for this version. If
stable behavior is required, use and test the extraction-and-shift variant instead.
Preservation should compare record identities or full multiplicities, not just sets of keys. The
algorithm's n-1 swap upper bound also supplies an instrumentation check for the guarded
implementation.

Supplement S3.8   Selection sort
S3.8 Selection sort: deep questions and neighboring concepts
Why must the suffix be scanned even if the prefix is ordered?
An ordered prefix is already finalized by the invariant, but the next smallest key can be
anywhere in the suffix. Without extra information about key values or their arrangement, every
candidate can affect which record must be selected. The fixed scan therefore performs the same
number of comparisons on ordered and disordered input.
Why do n-1 passes suffice?
After n-1 passes, the prefix contains the n-1 smallest records in order, every remaining key is no
smaller than the prefix, and exactly one record remains. That record necessarily occupies the
final position. A last minimum search on a singleton provides no new information.
Selection sort versus selecting one rank
The name selection sort does not mean an optimal selection algorithm for the kth smallest
element. Sorting the entire array is more work than needed if only one rank is requested. After k
passes, ordinary selection has finalized the k smallest records, but this partial method costs
O(kn) comparisons and is not a general linear-time rank-selection guarantee.
Selection versus insertion
Selection finds an extremum in the unresolved suffix and finalizes a boundary record. Insertion
takes the next record from the original processing order and inserts it into a sorted processed
prefix. A selection prefix is globally smallest; an insertion prefix need not be. Both can use
constant auxiliary storage, yet their adaptivity and stability rules differ.
Selection versus bubble
One long-distance selection swap may remove many inversions and may cross equal-key
identities. Each strict adjacent bubble swap removes exactly one inversion and preserves
equal-key order. An answer based only on "both move the minimum" overlooks these
consequences.

Getting Started
This chapter will familiarize you with the framework we shall use throughout the
book to think about the design and analysis of algorithms. It is self-contained, but
it does include several references to material that we introduce in Chapters 3 and 4.
(It also contains several summations, which Appendix A shows how to solve.)
We begin by examining the insertion sort algorithm to solve the sorting problem
introduced in Chapter 1. We deﬁne a “pseudocode” that should be familiar to you if
you have done computer programming, and we use it to show how we shall specify
our algorithms. Having speciﬁed the insertion sort algorithm, we then argue that it
correctly sorts, and we analyze its running time. The analysis introduces a notation
that focuses on how that time increases with the number of items to be sorted.
Following our discussion of insertion sort, we introduce the divide-and-conquer
approach to the design of algorithms and use it to develop an algorithm called
merge sort. We end with an analysis of merge sort’s running time.
2.1
Insertion sort
Our ﬁrst algorithm, insertion sort, solves the sorting problem introduced in Chap-
ter 1:
Input: A sequence of n numbers ⟨a₁, a₂, . . . , aₙ⟩.
Output: A permutation (reordering) ⟨a′
1, a′
2, . . . , a′
n⟩ of the input sequence such
that a′
1 ≤ a′
2 ≤ · · · ≤ a′
n.
The numbers that we wish to sort are also known as the keys. Although conceptu-
ally we are sorting a sequence, the input comes to us in the form of an array with n
elements.

reading our algorithms. What separates pseudocode from “real” code is that in
pseudocode, we employ whatever expressive method is most clear and concise to
specify a given algorithm. Sometimes, the clearest method is English, so do not
be surprised if you come across an English phrase or sentence embedded within
a section of “real” code. Another difference between pseudocode and real code
is that pseudocode is not typically concerned with issues of software engineering.
Issues of data abstraction, modularity, and error handling are often ignored in order
to convey the essence of the algorithm more concisely.
We start with insertion sort, which is an efﬁcient algorithm for sorting a small
number of elements. Insertion sort works the way many people sort a hand of
playing cards. We start with an empty left hand and the cards face down on the
table. We then remove one card at a time from the table and insert it into the
correct position in the left hand. To ﬁnd the correct position for a card, we compare
it with each of the cards already in the hand, from right to left, as illustrated in
Figure 2.1. At all times, the cards held in the left hand are sorted, and these cards
were originally the top cards of the pile on the table.
We present our pseudocode for insertion sort as a procedure called INSERTION-
SORT, which takes as a parameter an array A[1 . . n] containing a sequence of
length n that is to be sorted. (In the code, the number n of elements in A is denoted
by A.length.) The algorithm sorts the input numbers in place: it rearranges the
numbers within the array A, with at most a constant number of them stored outside
the array at any time. The input array A contains the sorted output sequence when
the INSERTION-SORT procedure is ﬁnished.

Initialization: It is true prior to the ﬁrst iteration of the loop.
Maintenance: If it is true before an iteration of the loop, it remains true before the
next iteration.
Termination: When the loop terminates, the invariant gives us a useful property
that helps show that the algorithm is correct.
When the ﬁrst two properties hold, the loop invariant is true prior to every iteration
of the loop. (Of course, we are free to use established facts other than the loop
invariant itself to prove that the loop invariant remains true before each iteration.)
Note the similarity to mathematical induction, where to prove that a property holds,
you prove a base case and an inductive step. Here, showing that the invariant holds
before the ﬁrst iteration corresponds to the base case, and showing that the invariant
holds from iteration to iteration corresponds to the inductive step.
The third property is perhaps the most important one, since we are using the loop
invariant to show correctness. Typically, we use the loop invariant along with the
condition that caused the loop to terminate. The termination property differs from
how we usually use mathematical induction, in which we apply the inductive step
inﬁnitely; here, we stop the “induction” when the loop terminates.
Let us see how these properties hold for insertion sort.
Initialization: We start by showing that the loop invariant holds before the ﬁrst
loop iteration, when j = 2.1 The subarray A[1 . . j − 1], therefore, consists
of just the single element A[1], which is in fact the original element in A[1].
Moreover, this subarray is sorted (trivially, of course), which shows that the
loop invariant holds prior to the ﬁrst iteration of the loop.
Maintenance: Next, we tackle the second property: showing that each iteration
maintains the loop invariant. Informally, the body of the for loop works by
moving A[j − 1], A[j − 2], A[j − 3], and so on by one position to the right
until it ﬁnds the proper position for A[j ] (lines 4–7), at which point it inserts
the value of A[j ] (line 8). The subarray A[1 . . j ] then consists of the elements
originally in A[1 . . j ], but in sorted order. Incrementing j for the next iteration
of the for loop then preserves the loop invariant.
A more formal treatment of the second property would require us to state and
show a loop invariant for the while loop of lines 5–7. At this point, however,

informal analysis to show that the second property holds for the outer loop.
Termination: Finally, we examine what happens when the loop terminates. The
condition causing the for loop to terminate is that j > A.length = n. Because
each loop iteration increases j by 1, we must have j = n + 1 at that time.
Substituting n + 1 for j in the wording of loop invariant, we have that the
subarray A[1 . . n] consists of the elements originally in A[1 . . n], but in sorted
order. Observing that the subarray A[1 . . n] is the entire array, we conclude that
the entire array is sorted. Hence, the algorithm is correct.
We shall use this method of loop invariants to show correctness later in this
chapter and in other chapters as well.
Pseudocode conventions
We use the following conventions in our pseudocode.
•
Indentation indicates block structure. For example, the body of the for loop that
begins on line 1 consists of lines 2–8, and the body of the while loop that begins
on line 5 contains lines 6–7 but not line 8. Our indentation style applies to
if-else statements2 as well. Using indentation instead of conventional indicators
of block structure, such as begin and end statements, greatly reduces clutter
while preserving, or even enhancing, clarity.3
•
The looping constructs while, for, and repeat-until and the if-else conditional
construct have interpretations similar to those in C, C++, Java, Python, and
Pascal.4 In this book, the loop counter retains its value after exiting the loop,
unlike some situations that arise in C++, Java, and Pascal. Thus, immediately
after a for loop, the loop counter’s value is the value that ﬁrst exceeded the for
loop bound. We used this property in our correctness argument for insertion
sort. The for loop header in line 1 is for j = 2 to A.length, and so when
this loop terminates, j = A.length + 1 (or, equivalently, j = n + 1, since
n = A.length). We use the keyword to when a for loop increments its loop
2In an if-else statement, we indent else at the same level as its matching if. Although we omit the
keyword then, we occasionally refer to the portion executed when the test following if is true as a
then clause. For multiway tests, we use elseif for tests after the ﬁrst one.
3Each pseudocode procedure in this book appears on one page so that you will not have to discern
levels of indentation in code that is split across pages.
4Most block-structured languages have equivalent constructs, though the exact syntax may differ.
Python lacks repeat-until loops, and its for loops operate a little differently from the for loops in
this book.

The symbol “//” indicates that the remainder of the line is a comment.
•
A multiple assignment of the form i = j = e assigns to both variables i and j
the value of expression e; it should be treated as equivalent to the assignment
j = e followed by the assignment i = j .
•
Variables (such as i, j , and key) are local to the given procedure. We shall not
use global variables without explicit indication.
•
We access array elements by specifying the array name followed by the in-
dex in square brackets.
For example, A[i] indicates the ith element of the
array A. The notation “. .” is used to indicate a range of values within an ar-
ray. Thus, A[1 . . j ] indicates the subarray of A consisting of the j elements
A[1], A[2], . . . , A[j ].
•
We typically organize compound data into objects, which are composed of
attributes. We access a particular attribute using the syntax found in many
object-oriented programming languages: the object name, followed by a dot,
followed by the attribute name. For example, we treat an array as an object
with the attribute length indicating how many elements it contains. To specify
the number of elements in an array A, we write A.length.
We treat a variable representing an array or object as a pointer to the data rep-
resenting the array or object. For all attributes f of an object x, setting y = x
causes y.f to equal x.f. Moreover, if we now set x.f = 3, then afterward not
only does x.f equal 3, but y.f equals 3 as well. In other words, x and y point
to the same object after the assignment y = x.
Our attribute notation can “cascade.” For example, suppose that the attribute f
is itself a pointer to some type of object that has an attribute g. Then the notation
x.f.g is implicitly parenthesized as (x.f).g. In other words, if we had assigned
y = x.f, then x.f.g is the same as y.g.
Sometimes, a pointer will refer to no object at all. In this case, we give it the
special value NIL.
•
We pass parameters to a procedure by value: the called procedure receives its
own copy of the parameters, and if it assigns a value to a parameter, the change
is not seen by the calling procedure. When objects are passed, the pointer to
the data representing the object is copied, but the object’s attributes are not. For
example, if x is a parameter of a called procedure, the assignment x = y within
the called procedure is not visible to the calling procedure. The assignment

•
A return statement immediately transfers control back to the point of call in
the calling procedure. Most return statements also take a value to pass back to
the caller. Our pseudocode differs from many programming languages in that
we allow multiple values to be returned in a single return statement.
•
The boolean operators “and” and “or” are short circuiting. That is, when we
evaluate the expression “x and y” we ﬁrst evaluate x. If x evaluates to FALSE,
then the entire expression cannot evaluate to TRUE, and so we do not evaluate y.
If, on the other hand, x evaluates to TRUE, we must evaluate y to determine the
value of the entire expression. Similarly, in the expression “x or y” we eval-
uate the expression y only if x evaluates to FALSE. Short-circuiting operators
allow us to write boolean expressions such as “x ≠ NIL and x.f = y” without
worrying about what happens when we try to evaluate x.f when x is NIL.
•
The keyword error indicates that an error occurred because conditions were
wrong for the procedure to have been called. The calling procedure is respon-
sible for handling the error, and so we do not specify what action to take.

2.2
Analyzing algorithms
Analyzing an algorithm has come to mean predicting the resources that the algo-
rithm requires. Occasionally, resources such as memory, communication band-
width, or computer hardware are of primary concern, but most often it is compu-
tational time that we want to measure. Generally, by analyzing several candidate
algorithms for a problem, we can identify a most efﬁcient one. Such analysis may
indicate more than one viable candidate, but we can often discard several inferior
algorithms in the process.
Before we can analyze an algorithm, we must have a model of the implemen-
tation technology that we will use, including a model for the resources of that
technology and their costs. For most of this book, we shall assume a generic one-
processor, random-access machine (RAM) model of computation as our imple-
mentation technology and understand that our algorithms will be implemented as
computer programs. In the RAM model, instructions are executed one after an-
other, with no concurrent operations.
Strictly speaking, we should precisely deﬁne the instructions of the RAM model
and their costs. To do so, however, would be tedious and would yield little insight
into algorithm design and analysis. Yet we must be careful not to abuse the RAM
model. For example, what if a RAM had an instruction that sorts? Then we could
sort in just one instruction. Such a RAM would be unrealistic, since real computers
do not have such instructions. Our guide, therefore, is how real computers are de-
signed. The RAM model contains instructions commonly found in real computers:
arithmetic (such as add, subtract, multiply, divide, remainder, ﬂoor, ceiling), data
movement (load, store, copy), and control (conditional and unconditional branch,
subroutine call and return). Each such instruction takes a constant amount of time.
The data types in the RAM model are integer and ﬂoating point (for storing real
numbers). Although we typically do not concern ourselves with precision in this
book, in some applications precision is crucial. We also assume a limit on the size
of each word of data. For example, when working with inputs of size n, we typ-
ically assume that integers are represented by c lg n bits for some constant c ≥ 1.
We require c ≥ 1 so that each word can hold the value of n, enabling us to index the
individual input elements, and we restrict c to be a constant so that the word size
does not grow arbitrarily. (If the word size could grow arbitrarily, we could store
huge amounts of data in one word and operate on it all in constant time—clearly
an unrealistic scenario.)

Chapter 2
Getting Started
Real computers contain instructions not listed above, and such instructions rep-
resent a gray area in the RAM model. For example, is exponentiation a constant-
time instruction? In the general case, no; it takes several instructions to compute xʸ
when x and y are real numbers. In restricted situations, however, exponentiation is
a constant-time operation. Many computers have a “shift left” instruction, which
in constant time shifts the bits of an integer by k positions to the left. In most
computers, shifting the bits of an integer by one position to the left is equivalent
to multiplication by 2, so that shifting the bits by k positions to the left is equiv-
alent to multiplication by 2k. Therefore, such computers can compute 2k in one
constant-time instruction by shifting the integer 1 by k positions to the left, as long
as k is no more than the number of bits in a computer word. We will endeavor to
avoid such gray areas in the RAM model, but we will treat computation of 2k as a
constant-time operation when k is a small enough positive integer.
In the RAM model, we do not attempt to model the memory hierarchy that is
common in contemporary computers. That is, we do not model caches or virtual
memory. Several computational models attempt to account for memory-hierarchy
effects, which are sometimes signiﬁcant in real programs on real machines. A
handful of problems in this book examine memory-hierarchy effects, but for the
most part, the analyses in this book will not consider them. Models that include
the memory hierarchy are quite a bit more complex than the RAM model, and so
they can be difﬁcult to work with. Moreover, RAM-model analyses are usually
excellent predictors of performance on actual machines.
Analyzing even a simple algorithm in the RAM model can be a challenge. The
mathematical tools required may include combinatorics, probability theory, alge-
braic dexterity, and the ability to identify the most signiﬁcant terms in a formula.
Because the behavior of an algorithm may be different for each possible input, we
need a means for summarizing that behavior in simple, easily understood formulas.
Even though we typically select only one machine model to analyze a given al-
gorithm, we still face many choices in deciding how to express our analysis. We
would like a way that is simple to write and manipulate, shows the important char-
acteristics of an algorithm’s resource requirements, and suppresses tedious details.
Analysis of insertion sort
The time taken by the INSERTION-SORT procedure depends on the input: sorting a
thousand numbers takes longer than sorting three numbers. Moreover, INSERTION-
SORT can take different amounts of time to sort two input sequences of the same
size depending on how nearly sorted they already are. In general, the time taken
by an algorithm grows with the size of the input, so it is traditional to describe the
running time of a program as a function of the size of its input. To do so, we need
to deﬁne the terms “running time” and “size of input” more carefully.

2.2
Analyzing algorithms
25
The best notion for input size depends on the problem being studied. For many
problems, such as sorting or computing discrete Fourier transforms, the most nat-
ural measure is the number of items in the input—for example, the array size n
for sorting. For many other problems, such as multiplying two integers, the best
measure of input size is the total number of bits needed to represent the input in
ordinary binary notation. Sometimes, it is more appropriate to describe the size of
the input with two numbers rather than one. For instance, if the input to an algo-
rithm is a graph, the input size can be described by the numbers of vertices and
edges in the graph. We shall indicate which input size measure is being used with
each problem we study.
The running time of an algorithm on a particular input is the number of primitive
operations or “steps” executed. It is convenient to deﬁne the notion of step so
that it is as machine-independent as possible. For the moment, let us adopt the
following view. A constant amount of time is required to execute each line of our
pseudocode. One line may take a different amount of time than another line, but
we shall assume that each execution of the ith line takes time cᵢ, where cᵢ is a
constant. This viewpoint is in keeping with the RAM model, and it also reﬂects
how the pseudocode would be implemented on most actual computers.5
In the following discussion, our expression for the running time of INSERTION-
SORT will evolve from a messy formula that uses all the statement costs cᵢ to a
much simpler notation that is more concise and more easily manipulated. This
simpler notation will also make it easy to determine whether one algorithm is more
efﬁcient than another.
We start by presenting the INSERTION-SORT procedure with the time “cost”
of each statement and the number of times each statement is executed. For each
j = 2, 3, . . . , n, where n = A.length, we let tj denote the number of times the
while loop test in line 5 is executed for that value of j . When a for or while loop

Worst-case and average-case analysis
In our analysis of insertion sort, we looked at both the best case, in which the input
array was already sorted, and the worst case, in which the input array was reverse
sorted. For the remainder of this book, though, we shall usually concentrate on
ﬁnding only the worst-case running time, that is, the longest running time for any
input of size n. We give three reasons for this orientation.
•
The worst-case running time of an algorithm gives us an upper bound on the
running time for any input. Knowing it provides a guarantee that the algorithm
will never take any longer. We need not make some educated guess about the
running time and hope that it never gets much worse.
•
For some algorithms, the worst case occurs fairly often. For example, in search-
ing a database for a particular piece of information, the searching algorithm’s
worst case will often occur when the information is not present in the database.
In some applications, searches for absent information may be frequent.

28
Chapter 2
Getting Started
•
The “average case” is often roughly as bad as the worst case. Suppose that we
randomly choose n numbers and apply insertion sort. How long does it take to
determine where in subarray A[1 . . j − 1] to insert element A[j ]? On average,
half the elements in A[1 . . j − 1] are less than A[j ], and half the elements are
greater. On average, therefore, we check half of the subarray A[1 . . j − 1], and
so tj is about j/2. The resulting average-case running time turns out to be a
quadratic function of the input size, just like the worst-case running time.
In some particular cases, we shall be interested in the average-case running time
of an algorithm; we shall see the technique of probabilistic analysis applied to
various algorithms throughout this book. The scope of average-case analysis is
limited, because it may not be apparent what constitutes an “average” input for
a particular problem. Often, we shall assume that all inputs of a given size are
equally likely. In practice, this assumption may be violated, but we can sometimes
use a randomized algorithm, which makes random choices, to allow a probabilistic
analysis and yield an expected running time. We explore randomized algorithms
more in Chapter 5 and in several other subsequent chapters.
Order of growth
We used some simplifying abstractions to ease our analysis of the INSERTION-
SORT procedure. First, we ignored the actual cost of each statement, using the
constants cᵢ to represent these costs. Then, we observed that even these constants
give us more detail than we really need: we expressed the worst-case running time
as an² + bn + c for some constants a, b, and c that depend on the statement
costs cᵢ. We thus ignored not only the actual statement costs, but also the abstract
costs cᵢ.
We shall now make one more simplifying abstraction: it is the rate of growth,
or order of growth, of the running time that really interests us. We therefore con-
sider only the leading term of a formula (e.g., an²), since the lower-order terms are
relatively insigniﬁcant for large values of n. We also ignore the leading term’s con-
stant coefﬁcient, since constant factors are less signiﬁcant than the rate of growth
in determining computational efﬁciency for large inputs. For insertion sort, when
we ignore the lower-order terms and the leading term’s constant coefﬁcient, we are
left with the factor of n² from the leading term. We write that insertion sort has a
worst-case running time of Θ(n²) (pronounced “theta of n-squared”). We shall use
Θ-notation informally in this chapter, and we will deﬁne it precisely in Chapter 3.
We usually consider one algorithm to be more efﬁcient than another if its worst-
case running time has a lower order of growth. Due to constant factors and lower-
order terms, an algorithm whose running time has a higher order of growth might

Supplement S4.1   Insertion sort
S4.1 Insertion sort: the saved key and the temporary hole
Processed order rather than global selection
Insertion sort takes the next input record, saves it, and inserts it into the ordered processed
prefix. It shifts larger records one position to the right until the saved key can be placed after
every key no greater than it. The untouched suffix contains records not yet processed.
The saved record is essential because the first shift overwrites its original slot. During shifting,
the array may temporarily contain a duplicate of a shifted record and omit the saved record; the
saved variable accounts for the missing identity. Preservation should be stated over the array
together with this saved record and the temporary hole, not naively over every intermediate
array state.
One insertion in detail
For [2,4,5 | 1,3], save 1. Shift 5 from position 2 to 3, shift 4 from 1 to 2, and shift 2 from 0 to 1.
Write saved 1 at position 0, giving [1,2,4,5 | 3]. A single insertion can move a key across the
whole prefix.
Zero-based procedure
INSERTION(A)
  for j = 1 to length(A)-1
    saved = A[j]
    i = j-1
    while i >= 0 and key(A[i]) > key(saved)
      A[i+1] = A[i]
      i = i-1
    A[i+1] = saved
The boundary check must be evaluated before reading A[i] when i becomes negative. Strict >
keeps an existing equal-key record before the newly inserted one and therefore gives stability.

Supplement S4.2   Insertion sort
S4.2 Insertion sort: inversions and adaptive running time
A sharper parameter than input length alone
Let I be the number of strict inversions in the initial array. In the shift-based insertion routine,
each larger predecessor shifted past the saved record corresponds to one inversion involving that
record. Every inversion is resolved exactly once during processing. The total number of shifts is
therefore I.
There are n-1 outer iterations. Each iteration has a constant amount of work plus its shifts and
associated key comparisons. Consequently running time is Theta(n+I) for n>=1 under the
constant-cost model, with the empty case handled separately. The key-comparison count is at
least I and at most I+n-1; a final unsuccessful key comparison may or may not occur, depending
on whether the left boundary is reached.
Important cases
An already ordered input has I=0 and takes Theta(n) time. Distinct reverse order has I=n(n-1)/2
and takes Theta(n^2). Under a uniform random permutation of distinct keys, E[I]=n(n-1)/4,
producing expected quadratic time.
For [2,3,...,n,1], there are n-1 inversions and one insertion shifts the whole preceding prefix, so
the total is Theta(n). For [n,1,2,...,n-1], each of the following records crosses the initial
maximum once; I is also n-1 and total time is linear. This is a stronger adaptivity guarantee than
a vague claim about "nearly sorted" data.
Counts are not identical
Each shift is one array write. The listing also writes the saved record once per outer iteration,
giving I+(n-1) array-slot writes, even if the saved record is written back to its unchanged
position. A guarded optimization can reduce some writes but changes the exact count.

Supplement S4.3   Insertion sort
S4.3 Insertion sort: ties, binary search, and data structures
Stable placement among equals
Shift a predecessor only if its key is strictly greater than the saved key. Thus the new record is
placed after the existing equal-key records. Replacing > with >= moves old equal records right
and can reverse tie order. A descending stable version reverses the strict direction but retains the
same no-crossing rule for equals.
Binary insertion separates search from movement
The insertion location can be found by binary search in the ordered prefix. To preserve stability,
choose the position after all existing equal keys, often called an upper-bound position. Finding
the location costs O(log j) comparisons for a prefix of size j, but shifting the intervening array
records can still take O(j) writes.
Over all insertions, binary search can reduce worst-case comparisons to O(n log n) while total
movement remains Theta(n^2) in reverse order. Binary insertion therefore does not turn a
standard contiguous-array insertion sorter into an O(n log n) total-time algorithm under a model
counting each moved record.
Arrays and linked lists
An array supports constant-time indexed access, but inserting into its middle requires moving
records. A linked list may insert at a known node position by changing a constant number of
links, yet locating that position can still require a linear traversal. Binary search is not
automatically logarithmic time on a singly linked list, because accessing the middle is not
constant time.
An incremental insertion sorter can process arriving records into an ordered collection. For an
array, that still entails shifting and capacity management. Calling the method online does not
remove its worst-case cost per insertion.

Supplement S4.4   Insertion sort
S4.4 Insertion sort: implementation and proof obligations
In-place stable implementation
def insertion_sort(a, key=lambda x: x):
    for j in range(1, len(a)):
        saved = a[j]
        saved_key = key(saved)
        i = j-1
        while i >= 0 and key(a[i]) > saved_key:
            a[i+1] = a[i]
            i -= 1
        a[i+1] = saved
    return a
Outer correctness argument
Before iteration j, the prefix a[0..j-1] contains exactly the first j original records, in stable sorted
order. Initialization holds for a singleton prefix. The iteration saves the next record and moves
only the suffix of larger prefix records. Placing saved at i+1 produces the ordered prefix
including that record; strict comparison preserves earlier equal records before it.
The loop counter advances through a finite list. The inner counter decreases and is bounded
below by -1, so termination holds. The saved record and shifted block restore the same
collection of processed records after every completed insertion. At the end the entire input has
been processed, proving sortedness, preservation, and stability.
Trace and failure checks
For [5,2,4,6,1,3], the completed prefixes grow as [2,5], [2,4,5], [2,4,5,6], [1,2,4,5,6], and
[1,2,3,4,5,6]. There are nine strict inversions and nine shifts. Check the final saved-key
placement even when no shifts occur; omitting it is dangerous after a nonempty shifting loop.
Boundary evaluation matters in Python: a[-1] is a valid access to the last element, so testing the
key before i>=0 can produce a logically wrong comparison instead of an immediate bounds
exception. Other languages may fail outright. The listed short-circuit order prevents that access.

text:
71
Supplement S4.5   Insertion sort
S4.5 Insertion sort: deep questions and hybrid use
Why is insertion useful inside a merge-based algorithm?
Small subarrays can be sorted with insertion before merges combine them. For subarray size t,
sorting approximately n/t blocks costs O(nt) in the worst case. Merging these blocks across
about log2(n/t) levels costs O(n log(n/t)). With a fixed small t, the complete method retains an
O(n log n) worst-case bound.
The practical threshold is not a universal constant. It depends on implementation, key costs,
memory access, and overhead. A teaching example can explain the formula without presenting
an unmeasured cutoff as a performance recommendation.
Does stable insertion repair an unstable merge?
No. Stability of the whole hybrid requires stability of the block sorts and every subsequent
merge. If a merge takes from the right on equal keys, it can undo the tie order established inside
and between blocks. Conversely, stable merge cannot repair arbitrary equal-key reversals
already caused by an unstable block sort.
Why not use insertion for every large input?
Its adaptive Theta(n+I) behavior is excellent when I is small, but I can be quadratic. A
worst-case guarantee must account for reverse or otherwise highly inverted data. A statement
based on one ordered benchmark does not establish the bound for arbitrary inputs.
Question bank
"How is insertion different from bubble?" It saves one record and shifts the larger prefix
segment; bubble repeatedly exchanges adjacent pairs in passes. "Does insertion know the global
minimum?" Not before processing all records. "Why is its best case linear?" Every new key
immediately satisfies the placement condition after a constant amount of work. "Can binary
insertion beat the comparison lower bound?" No; its worst-case comparison cost is O(n log n),
and it still has quadratic array movement in the worst case.
A proof-focused answer
For a proposed optimization, state the new invariant and re-count comparisons and writes
separately. Keeping the same final output is not enough to justify a claimed running-time
improvement, and matching a trace on one input is not enough to establish correctness on all
valid inputs.

Chapter 2
Getting Started
2.3.1
The divide-and-conquer approach
Many useful algorithms are recursive in structure: to solve a given problem, they
call themselves recursively one or more times to deal with closely related sub-
problems. These algorithms typically follow a divide-and-conquer approach: they
break the problem into several subproblems that are similar to the original prob-
lem but smaller in size, solve the subproblems recursively, and then combine these
solutions to create a solution to the original problem.
The divide-and-conquer paradigm involves three steps at each level of the recur-
sion:
Divide the problem into a number of subproblems that are smaller instances of the
same problem.
Conquer the subproblems by solving them recursively. If the subproblem sizes are
small enough, however, just solve the subproblems in a straightforward manner.
Combine the solutions to the subproblems into the solution for the original prob-
lem.
The merge sort algorithm closely follows the divide-and-conquer paradigm. In-
tuitively, it operates as follows.
Divide: Divide the n-element sequence to be sorted into two subsequences of n/2
elements each.
Conquer: Sort the two subsequences recursively using merge sort.
Combine: Merge the two sorted subsequences to produce the sorted answer.
The recursion “bottoms out” when the sequence to be sorted has length 1, in which
case there is no work to be done, since every sequence of length 1 is already in
sorted order.
The key operation of the merge sort algorithm is the merging of two sorted
sequences in the “combine” step. We merge by calling an auxiliary procedure
MERGE(A, p, q, r), where A is an array and p, q, and r are indices into the array
such that p ≤ q < r. The procedure assumes that the subarrays A[p . . q] and
A[q + 1 . . r] are in sorted order. It merges them to form a single sorted subarray
that replaces the current subarray A[p . . r].
Our MERGE procedure takes time Θ(n), where n = r − p + 1 is the total
number of elements being merged, and it works as follows. Returning to our card-
playing motif, suppose we have two piles of cards face up on a table. Each pile is
sorted, with the smallest cards on top. We wish to merge the two piles into a single
sorted output pile, which is to be face down on the table. Our basic step consists
of choosing the smaller of the two cards on top of the face-up piles, removing it

the output pile. We repeat this step until one input pile is empty, at which time
we just take the remaining input pile and place it face down onto the output pile.
Computationally, each basic step takes constant time, since we are comparing just
the two top cards. Since we perform at most n basic steps, merging takes Θ(n)
time.
The following pseudocode implements the above idea, but with an additional
twist that avoids having to check whether either pile is empty in each basic step.
We place on the bottom of each pile a sentinel card, which contains a special value
that we use to simplify our code. Here, we use ∞ as the sentinel value, so that
whenever a card with ∞ is exposed, it cannot be the smaller card unless both piles
have their sentinel cards exposed. But once that happens, all the nonsentinel cards
have already been placed onto the output pile. Since we know in advance that
exactly r − p + 1 cards will be placed onto the output pile, we can stop once we
have performed that many basic steps.

At the start of each iteration of the for loop of lines 12–17, the subarray
A[p . . k − 1] contains the k − p smallest elements of L[1 . . n₁ + 1] and
R[1 . . n₂ + 1], in sorted order. Moreover, L[i] and R[j ] are the smallest
elements of their arrays that have not been copied back into A.
We must show that this loop invariant holds prior to the ﬁrst iteration of the for
loop of lines 12–17, that each iteration of the loop maintains the invariant, and
that the invariant provides a useful property to show correctness when the loop
terminates.
Initialization: Prior to the ﬁrst iteration of the loop, we have k = p, so that the
subarray A[p . . k − 1] is empty. This empty subarray contains the k − p = 0
smallest elements of L and R, and since i = j = 1, both L[i] and R[j ] are the
smallest elements of their arrays that have not been copied back into A.

Termination: At termination, k = r + 1. By the loop invariant, the subarray
A[p . . k − 1], which is A[p . . r], contains the k − p = r − p + 1 smallest
elements of L[1 . . n₁ + 1] and R[1 . . n₂ + 1], in sorted order. The arrays L
and R together contain n₁ + n₂ + 2 = r − p + 3 elements. All but the two
largest have been copied back into A, and these two largest elements are the
sentinels.

We can now use the MERGE procedure as a subroutine in the merge sort al-
gorithm. The procedure MERGE-SORT(A, p, r) sorts the elements in the subar-
ray A[p . . r]. If p ≥ r, the subarray has at most one element and is therefore
already sorted. Otherwise, the divide step simply computes an index q that par-
titions A[p . . r] into two subarrays: A[p . . q], containing ⌈n/2⌉ elements, and
A[q + 1 . . r], containing ⌊n/2⌋ elements.8

To sort the entire sequence A = ⟨A[1], A[2], . . . , A[n]⟩, we make the initial call
MERGE-SORT(A, 1, A.length), where once again A.length = n. Figure 2.4 il-
lustrates the operation of the procedure bottom-up when n is a power of 2. The
algorithm consists of merging pairs of 1-item sequences to form sorted sequences
of length 2, merging pairs of sequences of length 2 to form sorted sequences of
length 4, and so on, until two sequences of length n/2 are merged to form the ﬁnal
sorted sequence of length n.
2.3.2
Analyzing divide-and-conquer algorithms
When an algorithm contains a recursive call to itself, we can often describe its
running time by a recurrence equation or recurrence, which describes the overall
running time on a problem of size n in terms of the running time on smaller inputs.
We can then use mathematical tools to solve the recurrence and provide bounds on
the performance of the algorithm.

A recurrence for the running time of a divide-and-conquer algorithm falls out
from the three steps of the basic paradigm. As before, we let T (n) be the running
time on a problem of size n. If the problem size is small enough, say n ≤ c
for some constant c, the straightforward solution takes constant time, which we
write as Θ(1). Suppose that our division of the problem yields a subproblems,
each of which is 1/b the size of the original. (For merge sort, both a and b are 2,
but we shall see many divide-and-conquer algorithms in which a ≠ b.) It takes
time T (n/b) to solve one subproblem of size n/b, and so it takes time aT (n/b)
to solve a of them. If we take D(n) time to divide the problem into subproblems
and C(n) time to combine the solutions to the subproblems into the solution to the
original problem, we get the recurrence
T (n) =

Θ(1)
if n ≤ c ,
aT (n/b) + D(n) + C(n)
otherwise .

quences of size exactly n/2. In Chapter 4, we shall see that this assumption does
not affect the order of growth of the solution to the recurrence.
We reason as follows to set up the recurrence for T (n), the worst-case running
time of merge sort on n numbers. Merge sort on just one element takes constant
time. When we have n > 1 elements, we break down the running time as follows.
Divide: The divide step just computes the middle of the subarray, which takes
constant time. Thus, D(n) = Θ(1).
Conquer: We recursively solve two subproblems, each of size n/2, which con-
tributes 2T (n/2) to the running time.
Combine: We have already noted that the MERGE procedure on an n-element
subarray takes time Θ(n), and so C(n) = Θ(n).
When we add the functions D(n) and C(n) for the merge sort analysis, we are
adding a function that is Θ(n) and a function that is Θ(1). This sum is a linear
function of n, that is, Θ(n). Adding it to the 2T (n/2) term from the “conquer”
step gives the recurrence for the worst-case running time T (n) of merge sort:
T (n) =
{
Θ(1)
if n = 1 ,
2T (n/2) + Θ(n)
if n > 1 .
(2.1)
In Chapter 4, we shall see the “master theorem,” which we can use to show
that T (n) is Θ(n lg n), where lg n stands for log2 n. Because the logarithm func-
tion grows more slowly than any linear function, for large enough inputs, merge
sort, with its Θ(n lg n) running time, outperforms insertion sort, whose running
time is Θ(n²), in the worst case.
We do not need the master theorem to intuitively understand why the solution to
the recurrence (2.1) is T (n) = Θ(n lg n). Let us rewrite recurrence (2.1) as

and the time per array element of the divide and combine steps. We can get around this problem by
letting c be the larger of these times and understanding that our recurrence gives an upper bound on
the running time, or by letting c be the lesser of these times and understanding that our recurrence
gives a lower bound on the running time. Both bounds are on the order of n lg n and, taken together,
give a Θ(n lg n) running time.

Designing algorithms

Figure 2.5 shows how we can solve recurrence (2.2). For convenience, we as-
sume that n is an exact power of 2. Part (a) of the ﬁgure shows T (n), which we
expand in part (b) into an equivalent tree representing the recurrence. The cn term
is the root (the cost incurred at the top level of recursion), and the two subtrees of
the root are the two smaller recurrences T (n/2). Part (c) shows this process carried
one step further by expanding T (n/2). The cost incurred at each of the two sub-
nodes at the second level of recursion is cn/2. We continue expanding each node
in the tree by breaking it into its constituent parts as determined by the recurrence,
until the problem sizes get down to 1, each with a cost of c. Part (d) shows the
resulting recursion tree.
Next, we add the costs across each level of the tree. The top level has total
cost cn, the next level down has total cost c(n/2) + c(n/2) = cn, the level after
that has total cost c(n/4)+c(n/4)+c(n/4)+c(n/4) = cn, and so on. In general,
the level i below the top has 2i nodes, each contributing a cost of c(n/2i), so that
the ith level below the top has total cost 2i c(n/2i) = cn. The bottom level has n
nodes, each contributing a cost of c, for a total cost of cn.
The total number of levels of the recursion tree in Figure 2.5 is lg n + 1, where
n is the number of leaves, corresponding to the input size. An informal inductive
argument justiﬁes this claim. The base case occurs when n = 1, in which case the
tree has only one level. Since lg 1 = 0, we have that lg n + 1 gives the correct
number of levels. Now assume as an inductive hypothesis that the number of levels
of a recursion tree with 2i leaves is lg 2i + 1 = i + 1 (since for any value of i,
we have that lg 2i = i). Because we are assuming that the input size is a power
of 2, the next input size to consider is 2i⁺¹. A tree with n = 2ⁱ⁺¹ leaves has
one more level than a tree with 2i leaves, and so the total number of levels is
(i + 1) + 1 = lg 2i⁺¹ + 1.
To compute the total cost represented by the recurrence (2.2), we simply add up
the costs of all the levels. The recursion tree has lg n + 1 levels, each costing cn,
for a total cost of cn(lg n + 1) = cn lg n + cn. Ignoring the low-order term and
the constant c gives the desired result of Θ(n lg n).

Chapter 2
Getting Started
b. What array with elements from the set {1, 2, . . . , n} has the most inversions?
How many does it have?
c. What is the relationship between the running time of insertion sort and the
number of inversions in the input array? Justify your answer.
d. Give an algorithm that determines the number of inversions in any permutation
on n elements in Θ(n lg n) worst-case time. (Hint: Modify merge sort.)
Chapter notes
In 1968, Knuth published the ﬁrst of three volumes with the general title The Art of
Computer Programming [209, 210, 211]. The ﬁrst volume ushered in the modern
study of computer algorithms with a focus on the analysis of running time, and the
full series remains an engaging and worthwhile reference for many of the topics
presented here. According to Knuth, the word “algorithm” is derived from the
name “al-Khowˆarizmˆı,” a ninth-century Persian mathematician.
Aho, Hopcroft, and Ullman [5] advocated the asymptotic analysis of algo-
rithms—using notations that Chapter 3 introduces, including Θ-notation—as a
means of comparing relative performance. They also popularized the use of re-
currence relations to describe the running times of recursive algorithms.
Knuth [211] provides an encyclopedic treatment of many sorting algorithms. His
comparison of sorting algorithms (page 381) includes exact step-counting analyses,
like the one we performed here for insertion sort. Knuth’s discussion of insertion
sort encompasses several variations of the algorithm. The most important of these
is Shell’s sort, introduced by D. L. Shell, which uses insertion sort on periodic
subsequences of the input to produce a faster sorting algorithm.
Merge sort is also described by Knuth. He mentions that a mechanical colla-
tor capable of merging two decks of punched cards in a single pass was invented
in 1938. J. von Neumann, one of the pioneers of computer science, apparently
wrote a program for merge sort on the EDVAC computer in 1945.
The early history of proving programs correct is described by Gries [153], who
credits P. Naur with the ﬁrst article in this ﬁeld. Gries attributes loop invariants to
R. W. Floyd. The textbook by Mitchell [256] describes more recent progress in
proving programs correct.

Supplement S5.1   Merge sort
S5.1 Merge sort: ranges, recursion, and recombination
Divide, conquer, and combine
Merge sort splits an input range into two smaller ranges, recursively sorts both, and merges the
ordered results. The split does not itself sort records. The combine step relies on both recursive
results already being ordered. A range containing zero or one record is the base case and needs
no rearrangement.
Half-open ranges
For zero-based indexing, use [lo,hi), which contains hi-lo records and excludes hi. Let
mid=lo+(hi-lo)//2. The children are [lo,mid) and [mid,hi); they do not overlap, and their union is
the parent range. Stop when hi-lo<=1.
The CLRS presentation uses one-based inclusive ranges. Its midpoint and recursion bounds are
correct under that convention. Translate the whole range contract rather than copying only one
endpoint formula into a half-open implementation.
A complete split pattern
For [5,1,4,2,8], split into [5,1] and [4,2,8]. The first child becomes [1,5]. The second splits into
[4] and [2,8], then merges into [2,4,8]. Merging the two children yields [1,2,4,5,8]. Odd lengths
are normal: the two child sizes differ by at most one.
Why recursion terminates
When the parent size exceeds one, both child sizes are smaller than the parent size. Repeated
halving eventually reaches a singleton. A missing base case or a midpoint that reproduces the
parent interval can cause infinite recursion.

Supplement S5.2   Merge sort
S5.2 The merge operation: a full two-pointer trace
The smallest available head
Let L=[1,4,7] and R=[2,4,6]. Initially both read pointers are zero and the output is empty.
Compare the heads and emit 1 from L. Then compare 4 and 2 and emit 2 from R. Compare the
two 4s and emit the left 4 first for stability. Compare 7 and the right 4 and emit the right 4.
Compare 7 and 6 and emit 6.
R is now exhausted. Append the remaining 7 from L without a key comparison. The output is
[1,2,4,4,6,7]. There were five key comparisons and six output writes. The key-comparison count
for nonempty runs of sizes a and b is at most a+b-1; copying the unconsumed remainder
supplies the rest of the writes.
Invariant for the output prefix
Before each comparison, the output contains exactly the already consumed records from L and
R in ordered form, and those records are no greater than every unconsumed record. Because
each input run is ordered, its head is its smallest unconsumed key. Choosing the smaller head
therefore selects a smallest remaining record overall.
Advance only the pointer for the run from which a record was emitted. Forgetting to advance
repeats a record and can prevent termination; advancing both can skip a record. When one run is
exhausted, the remaining records in the other run are already ordered and no smaller than the
output boundary.

Supplement S5.3   Merge sort
S5.3 Merge sort: time recurrences and memory accounting
A recurrence with uneven splits
For n>1, conventional merge sort satisfies T(n)=T(floor(n/2))+T(ceil(n/2))+Theta(n). The
Theta(n) combine term includes writing or copying all records in the parent range. For powers
of two this simplifies to T(n)=2T(n/2)+Theta(n), with a constant-time singleton base case.
Each nonleaf recursion level handles a total of n records. The tree has Theta(log n) levels, giving
Theta(n log n) total time for the conventional always-merge implementation. The input's
existing order does not remove the required copying work in this version. An optimized
implementation that checks the two-child boundary and skips an unnecessary merge can have a
different best case.
Peak auxiliary space
A reusable temporary array of size n needs O(n) records. The recursion stack has O(log n)
frames for balanced splitting. Together these are O(n) auxiliary space. If temporary child arrays
are created by slicing, account for their actual lifetimes; balanced depth-first recursion can still
have O(n) peak live element storage, while generating O(n log n) total allocation traffic over the
execution.
Do not add storage across time as though it were all live simultaneously. Conversely, retaining
every temporary version or every recursion-level snapshot for visualization can increase
memory and is a different implementation from a normal merge sort.
Comparison lower bound
A comparison decision tree for n distinct keys must distinguish n! orderings, so worst-case
height is at least log2(n!)=Omega(n log n). Merge sort matches this order of growth in the
comparison model. Counting sort uses value indexing and therefore operates outside that
lower-bound model.

Supplement S5.4   Merge sort
S5.4 Merge sort: a stable sentinel-free implementation
A fresh-output version
This listing returns a new list rather than sorting the caller's list in place. The recursive inputs are
slices; stability follows from stable recursion and left-first equality during each merge.
def merge_sort(a, key=lambda x: x):
    if len(a) <= 1:
        return list(a)
    mid = len(a)//2
    left = merge_sort(a[:mid], key)
    right = merge_sort(a[mid:], key)
    out = []
    i = j = 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if key(left[i]) <= key(right[j]):
            out.append(left[i]); i += 1
        else:
            out.append(right[j]); j += 1
    out.extend(left[i:])
    out.extend(right[j:])
    return out
Sentinels are a separate design
CLRS presents a merge using an infinity sentinel. A practical sentinel must be greater than
every permitted input key and compatible with the comparison domain. An ordinary maximum
integer is unsafe if that same value is a valid data key. A unique sentinel object also needs an
appropriate comparator. The listing above avoids those issues by testing whether either run is
exhausted.
Proof obligations and checks
The split ranges partition the original sequence, recursive results preserve their records, and
merge emits every record exactly once. The smaller-head invariant proves order. On equal keys,
left-first selection preserves records from the original left range before equal records from the
right; combined with stable child sorts, this gives global stability.
Check [], a singleton, odd lengths, duplicated labeled keys across both halves, and maximum
permitted keys. Do not use a mutation-based test expectation for this returning-a-new-list
contract.

Supplement S5.5   Merge sort
S5.5 Merge sort: stability, descending order, and adaptivity
Stability requires consistent tie handling
Every record in the original left half precedes every record in the original right half. When equal
keys are at both heads, choosing the left record preserves that relationship. If the child sorts are
stable and every merge uses this rule, an induction on recursion size proves the entire sort stable.
For descending order, choose the left head when its key is greater than or equal to the right head.
Equal records still come from the left first. Reversing a stable ascending output would reverse
tie groups and is therefore not a substitute for stable descending merging.
Skip a merge only when justified
After sorting both children, if the maximum left key is no greater than the minimum right key,
their concatenation is already ordered. With ascending ranges, check the last left record against
the first right record. Skipping the merge preserves stability because the left group's equal
records already precede the right group's.
For an implementation using indexed ranges and a reusable buffer, this boundary test can yield
Theta(n) best-case work on already ordered input: the recursion visits O(n) nodes and each
successful skip costs constant time. A version that still slices or copies whole sublists at every
level may retain Theta(n log n) copying cost even if it skips comparisons. State the
implementation before claiming linear best time.
Natural runs and bottom-up merging
Bottom-up merge sort combines runs of size 1, then 2, then 4, and so on, avoiding a recursive
stack while still needing an array merge buffer. A natural merge variant starts from detected
ordered runs and can exploit existing structure. These are distinct variants; do not apply the
standard recurrence blindly to every adaptive run strategy.

Supplement S5.6   Merge sort
S5.6 Merge sort: inversion counting as a derived application
Count pairs across the split
Each inversion belongs either entirely to the left range, entirely to the right range, or crosses the
split. Recursive calls count the first two classes. During an ascending merge, if right[j] is strictly
smaller than left[i], every remaining left record is greater than right[j], because the left run is
ordered. Add len(left)-i to the cross-inversion count when emitting that right record.
If left[i] is no greater than right[j], emit the left record without adding a crossing inversion.
Equality must not be counted as a strict inversion. The total count is left_count + right_count +
cross_count. This procedure has Theta(n log n) running time using the standard merge
recurrence.
A worked merge
For left=[2,4,5] and right=[1,3], emitting 1 from the right adds 3 crossing inversions: (2,1),
(4,1), and (5,1). Emit 2 from the left. Then emitting 3 from the right adds 2: (4,3) and (5,3). The
cross count is 5, and the merged output is [1,2,3,4,5].
The original array [2,4,5,1,3] has no inversions internal to either already ordered half, so its full
count is 5. If the halves were not originally ordered, their internal inversion counts must be
retained from the recursive calls rather than ignored.
Use the result carefully
The count measures pair disorder. It helps explain insertion-sort shifts and strict adjacent bubble
exchanges. It does not equal the number of selection-sort swaps, and it is not the number of
positions occupied by the wrong value.
For very large n, n(n-1)/2 can exceed a fixed-width integer's maximum. Choose a count
representation large enough for the contract. Python integers grow as needed, but their
arithmetic cost is not literally constant for arbitrarily large counts.

Supplement S5.7   Merge sort
S5.7 Merge sort: deep questions and practical boundaries
Can merge sort be in place?
The conventional array merge routine discussed here uses a linear auxiliary buffer and is not in
place under the O(1)-extra-storage definition. More sophisticated in-place merging methods
exist, but they have different implementations and tradeoffs. A statement about the standard
method should not claim that every possible merge sort necessarily requires the same buffer.
Linked-list merging can rearrange links rather than copy a linear array buffer, since it can
repeatedly take a run's head. Recursion frames, run bookkeeping, and output representation still
need accounting. "No array buffer" is not automatically "zero auxiliary space".
Why does merging help external sorting?
Ordered runs can be read sequentially and combined into another ordered stream. When records
do not fit memory, one can create memory-sized sorted runs and then merge them with bounded
input/output buffers. Disk I/O, number of runs, merge fan-in, and buffer sizes become important
cost parameters. The in-memory Theta(n log n) CPU bound alone does not specify an
external-sorting I/O bound.
Parallel work is not automatic speedup
The two child sorts concern disjoint ranges and can be performed independently. A sequential
merge still consumes time proportional to the parent range. Actual parallel speed depends on
task overhead, memory bandwidth, available workers, and whether merging is parallelized;
recursion alone does not establish a numeric speedup.
Question bank
"Why is merge sort better than insertion for large disordered input?" Its worst-case growth is n
log n rather than quadratic, under the stated model. "Why might insertion win on a small input?"
Lower overhead and few shifts can outweigh the asymptotic distinction. "Why doesn't counting
sort violate merge's optimality?" Optimality applies within the comparison model, while
counting uses a restricted integer domain and value-indexed storage.
Answering a variant question
State whether the routine is top-down or bottom-up, array or list based, stable or right-first on
ties, buffered or using a special in-place merge, and adaptive or always merging. These choices
control both guarantees and trace interpretation.

What about a fraction 1/2n?
8.1-4
Suppose that you are given a sequence of n elements to sort. The input sequence
consists of n/k subsequences, each containing k elements. The elements in a given
subsequence are all smaller than the elements in the succeeding subsequence and
larger than the elements in the preceding subsequence. Thus, all that is needed to
sort the whole sequence of length n is to sort the k elements in each of the n/k
subsequences. Show an Ω(n lg k) lower bound on the number of comparisons
needed to solve this variant of the sorting problem. (Hint: It is not rigorous to
simply combine the lower bounds for the individual subsequences.)
8.2
Counting sort
Counting sort assumes that each of the n input elements is an integer in the range
0 to k, for some integer k. When k = O(n), the sort runs in Θ(n) time.
Counting sort determines, for each input element x, the number of elements less
than x. It uses this information to place element x directly into its position in the
output array. For example, if 17 elements are less than x, then x belongs in output
position 18. We must modify this scheme slightly to handle the situation in which
several elements have the same value, since we do not want to put them all in the
same position.
In the code for counting sort, we assume that the input is an array A[1 . . n], and
thus A.length = n. We require two other arrays: the array B[1 . . n] holds the
sorted output, and the array C[0 . . k] provides temporary working storage.

Chapter 8
Sorting in Linear Time
Finally, the for loop of lines 10–12 places each element A[j ] into its correct
sorted position in the output array B. If all n elements are distinct, then when we
ﬁrst enter line 10, for each A[j ], the value C[A[j ]] is the correct ﬁnal position
of A[j ] in the output array, since there are C[A[j ]] elements less than or equal
to A[j ]. Because the elements might not be distinct, we decrement C[A[j ]] each
time we place a value A[j ] into the B array. Decrementing C[A[j ]] causes the
next input element with a value equal to A[j ], if one exists, to go to the position
immediately before A[j ] in the output array.
How much time does counting sort require? The for loop of lines 2–3 takes
time Θ(k), the for loop of lines 4–5 takes time Θ(n), the for loop of lines 7–8 takes
time Θ(k), and the for loop of lines 10–12 takes time Θ(n). Thus, the overall time
is Θ(k + n). In practice, we usually use counting sort when we have k = O(n), in
which case the running time is Θ(n).
Counting sort beats the lower bound of Ω(n lg n) proved in Section 8.1 because
it is not a comparison sort. In fact, no comparisons between input elements occur
anywhere in the code. Instead, counting sort uses the actual values of the elements
to index into an array. The Ω(n lg n) lower bound for sorting does not apply when
we depart from the comparison sort model.
An important property of counting sort is that it is stable: numbers with the same
value appear in the output array in the same order as they do in the input array. That
is, it breaks ties between two numbers by the rule that whichever number appears
ﬁrst in the input array appears ﬁrst in the output array. Normally, the property of
stability is important only when satellite data are carried around with the element
being sorted. Counting sort’s stability is important for another reason: counting
sort is often used as a subroutine in radix sort. As we shall see in the next section,
in order for radix sort to work correctly, counting sort must be stable.
Exercises
8.2-1
Using Figure 8.2 as a model, illustrate the operation of COUNTING-SORT on the
array A = ⟨6, 0, 2, 0, 1, 3, 4, 6, 1, 3, 2⟩.
8.2-2
Prove that COUNTING-SORT is stable.
8.2-3
Suppose that we were to rewrite the for loop header in line 10 of the COUNTING-
SORT as
10
for j = 1 to A.length
Show that the algorithm still works properly. Is the modiﬁed algorithm stable?

8.3
Radix sort
197
8.2-4
Describe an algorithm that, given n integers in the range 0 to k, preprocesses its
input and then answers any query about how many of the n integers fall into a
range [a . . b] in O(1) time. Your algorithm should use Θ(n + k) preprocessing
time.
8.3
Radix sort
Radix sort is the algorithm used by the card-sorting machines you now ﬁnd only in
computer museums. The cards have 80 columns, and in each column a machine can
punch a hole in one of 12 places. The sorter can be mechanically “programmed”
to examine a given column of each card in a deck and distribute the card into one
of 12 bins depending on which place has been punched. An operator can then
gather the cards bin by bin, so that cards with the ﬁrst place punched are on top of
cards with the second place punched, and so on.
For decimal digits, each column uses only 10 places. (The other two places
are reserved for encoding nonnumeric characters.) A d-digit number would then
occupy a ﬁeld of d columns. Since the card sorter can look at only one column
at a time, the problem of sorting n cards on a d-digit number requires a sorting
algorithm.
Intuitively, you might sort numbers on their most signiﬁcant digit, sort each of
the resulting bins recursively, and then combine the decks in order. Unfortunately,
since the cards in 9 of the 10 bins must be put aside to sort each of the bins, this
procedure generates many intermediate piles of cards that you would have to keep
track of. (See Exercise 8.3-5.)
Radix sort solves the problem of card sorting—counterintuitively—by sorting on
the least signiﬁcant digit ﬁrst. The algorithm then combines the cards into a single
deck, with the cards in the 0 bin preceding the cards in the 1 bin preceding the
cards in the 2 bin, and so on. Then it sorts the entire deck again on the second-least
signiﬁcant digit and recombines the deck in a like manner. The process continues
until the cards have been sorted on all d digits. Remarkably, at that point the cards
are fully sorted on the d-digit number. Thus, only d passes through the deck are
required to sort. Figure 8.3 shows how radix sort operates on a “deck” of seven
3-digit numbers.
In order for radix sort to work correctly, the digit sorts must be stable. The sort
performed by a card sorter is stable, but the operator has to be wary about not
changing the order of the cards as they come out of a bin, even though all the cards
in a bin have the same digit in the chosen column.

Supplement S6.1   Counting sort
S6.1 Counting sort: domain and range are part of the input
Integer keys with a manageable range
Counting sort exploits the fact that keys can index a finite array. For keys 0 through k inclusive,
the range has R=k+1 values. It counts occurrences, computes cumulative positions, and
distributes records directly into key-ordered output positions. It does not determine order by
pairwise comparisons of input records.
The inclusive range matters: keys 0 through 5 require six counters, not five. In the stable
output-array form, time is Theta(n+R) and auxiliary space is O(n+R). Calling this linear in n
requires R=O(n), or a fixed range under the chosen analysis. With ten keys whose maximum is a
billion, the range array is usually an inappropriate direct representation.
Two forms with different promises
A frequency-only numeric sort counts values and writes each value as many times as its
frequency. That can reconstruct sorted numeric values using O(R) counters when overwriting
the input, but it does not by itself preserve identities of records carrying satellite data.
Stable record counting sort uses an output array and a placement rule that preserves equal-key
arrival order. The algorithm explained in CLRS belongs to this form. Do not attach its stability
guarantee to a numeric frequency reconstruction routine unless the record handling has been
specified.
Mapping other domains
Negative integers can be offset by their minimum value. A finite categorical ordering can be
encoded as integer ranks if that rank order is explicitly defined. Arbitrary strings or
floating-point values cannot simply be used as count-array indices. A rank-compression
preprocessing step may require comparison sorting and must be counted separately.

Supplement S6.2   Counting sort
S6.2 Counting sort: histogram, cumulative counts, and positions
Histogram phase
Use A=[2,5,3,0,2,3,0,3], with keys 0 through 5. Initial frequencies are F=[2,0,2,3,0,1]. The entry
F[v] is the number of records whose key equals v, and the sum of all frequency entries is n=8.
Cumulative phase
Compute C[v]=F[0]+...+F[v], giving C=[2,2,4,7,7,8]. C[v] is the number of keys no greater than
v. It is nondecreasing, not a frequency histogram. In one-based output positions, key v ends at
position C[v]. In a zero-based output list, its current last available position is C[v]-1.
For key 3, seven records have keys <=3. Its final group occupies zero-based positions 4 through
6, since four keys are strictly smaller and three keys equal 3. Distinguish that interval from the
scalar C[3]=7.
Placement phase
Traverse A from right to left. The last 3 goes to B[6], then decrement C[3] from 7 to 6. The
preceding 0 goes to B[1], decrementing C[0] from 2 to 1. The preceding 3 goes to B[5], and
later the earliest 3 goes to B[4]. After all records are placed, B=[0,0,2,2,3,3,3,5].
The C array is consumed as a next-free-position structure. Its final values no longer represent
the original cumulative counts. If later range queries require the cumulative totals, preserve a
separate copy before placement.

Supplement S6.3   Counting sort
S6.3 Counting sort: stable placement and correctness
Disjoint reserved intervals
Let P[v] be the original cumulative number of keys <=v and let P[-1]=0 for the proof. Key v
owns the zero-based interval [P[v-1],P[v]). Its length is the frequency of v. Different keys have
disjoint intervals, and smaller keys own earlier intervals.
Initially C[v]=P[v]. Each placement of a key-v record writes to C[v]-1 and decrements C[v].
Thus it fills the reserved interval from right to left without collision. Exactly the key's frequency
many records are processed, so its interval is filled exactly once. Together the intervals fill all n
output positions and preserve every record.
Why reverse input traversal is stable
Suppose equal-key record x precedes y in the input. A right-to-left traversal processes y first,
placing it in a later available slot. When x is processed, the counter has moved left, so x receives
an earlier slot. Their output order is therefore the same as their input order.
If the same cumulative-end-position rule processes input left to right, x receives the later slot
and y the earlier slot. Numeric keys remain correctly sorted, but equal-key record identities are
reversed within their group. This answers the distinction in Exercise 8.2-3.
A different stable forward variant
Forward input traversal can still be stable if it uses starting positions rather than ending
positions. Initialize next[v] to the number of keys strictly smaller than v, write to B[next[v]],
then increment next[v]. The first equal record gets the first slot. Direction alone is not the proof;
direction and position-update rule must agree.

Supplement S6.4   Counting sort
S6.4 Counting sort: signed integers, sparse ranges, and space
Offset the key domain
For signed integer keys, let lo be the minimum and hi the maximum. Allocate R=hi-lo+1
counters and map a key x to index x-lo. The transformation preserves numeric order: x<y if and
only if x-lo<y-lo. Store full original records in the output, not merely the mapped indices.
For A=[-2,1,-2,0], lo=-2 and hi=1. The mapped indices are [0,3,0,2] and the frequencies are
[2,0,1,1]. Output records have keys [-2,-2,0,1]. Handle the empty list before requesting a
minimum or maximum.
Range size controls feasibility
Finding min and max costs Theta(n) and does not remove the O(R) initialization or cumulative
scan. A large gap between lo and hi creates counters for absent keys too. For keys
[-1000000,1000000], only two values occur but the direct range has 2000001 entries.
A hash-map histogram stores only observed keys, but producing globally ordered key groups
still requires ordering those keys or a separately known domain order. If m observed distinct
keys are comparison-sorted, that step costs O(m log m). It is not justified to call such a modified
method unconditional linear-time counting sort.
Space distinctions
The stable record version has O(n+R) extra storage for output and counts. A numeric
frequency-reconstruction version may overwrite the input and use O(R) counters, but it does not
preserve arbitrary satellite records. If a caller supplies a reusable output buffer, report whether
that buffer is included in the stated auxiliary-space measure.

Supplement S6.5   Counting sort
S6.5 Counting sort: a stable record implementation
Contract and implementation
This function returns a new list, accepts negative integer keys, and preserves input order among
equal keys. Its range allocation must fit the application's memory budget. This teaching
implementation assumes every extracted key is an integer; a production input validator should
enforce the stated domain.
def counting_sort(a, key=lambda x: x):
    if not a:
        return []
    keys = [key(x) for x in a]
    lo, hi = min(keys), max(keys)
    counts = [0] * (hi-lo+1)
    for k in keys:
        counts[k-lo] += 1
    for v in range(1, len(counts)):
        counts[v] += counts[v-1]
    out = [None] * len(a)
    for j in range(len(a)-1, -1, -1):
        v = keys[j]-lo
        counts[v] -= 1
        out[counts[v]] = a[j]
    return out
Decrementing immediately before the write is equivalent to writing at the old cumulative count
minus one and then decrementing. It is not an arbitrary off-by-one change. All array accesses
use zero-based positions and offset key indices.
Checks and cost
For [(2,'a'),(-1,'b'),(2,'c')], the first-field key gives [(-1,'b'),(2,'a'),(2,'c')]. The original list remains
in its original order. Every out slot must be filled; an unfilled None would expose a placement or
domain error.
Caching extracted keys costs O(n) additional storage beyond counts and output, but the total
remains O(n+R). The extraction, min/max, counting, and output passes are linear in n;
initialization and cumulative counting are linear in R. Empty input bypasses min/max and range
allocation.

Supplement S6.6   Counting sort
S6.6 Counting sort: range queries and radix-sort connections
Preprocess inclusive range counts
Let P[v] be the number of keys <=v before output placement consumes any counters. Define
count_le(x)=0 below the minimum allowed key and count_le(x)=n at or above the maximum.
Within the range, look up the corresponding cumulative entry.
The number of input keys in the inclusive interval [a,b] is count_le(b)-count_le(a-1) for integer
a<=b. If a>b, return zero by the query contract. Computing a histogram and its cumulative array
takes Theta(n+R); each subsequent valid interval query takes O(1) under machine-integer
indexing assumptions.
For [2,5,3,0,2,3,0,3], there are five values in [2,3]: P[3]-P[1]=7-2=5. There are two values in
[0,1], and zero in [4,4]. The inclusive subtraction boundary a-1 is crucial; P[b]-P[a] would
incorrectly exclude records equal to a.
Why a digit pass needs stability
Least-significant-digit radix sorting first orders the lowest digit, then successively more
significant digits. Each pass must preserve the order already established among records sharing
the current digit. A stable counting sort can be the digit-pass subroutine when the digit alphabet
is a small integer range.
For two-digit keys [21,11,12], the units pass produces [21,11,12], retaining 21 before 11 for the
shared units digit 1. A stable tens pass produces [11,12,21], preserving the units order within
tens group 1. An unstable tens pass could instead place 12 before 11 and lose the earlier work.
The full radix bound depends on digit count d and digit range R: a straightforward
implementation costs Theta(d(n+R)). The counting-sort bound alone does not make
arbitrary-width integer radix sorting linear without those parameters.

Supplement S6.7   Counting sort
S6.7 Counting sort: deep questions, limits, and corpus audit
Does linear counting sort contradict a lower bound?
No. The Omega(n log n) theorem applies to worst-case comparison sorting of arbitrary distinct
comparable keys, where ordering information comes only from pairwise comparisons. Counting
sort assumes bounded integer keys and uses their values to address an array. Those additional
operations and domain restrictions change the model.
Is it always the fastest of these five methods?
No. Theta(n+R) can be dominated by a huge R. Memory allocation, zero-initialization, payload
handling, key extraction, and the actual comparison cost all affect a concrete execution. A
domain and range check is necessary before choosing it. An asymptotic formula is not a
measured performance ranking.
Can it be stable and in place simultaneously?
The conventional CLRS stable record version uses an output array and is not O(1)-extra-space.
Numeric reconstruction may overwrite input values with O(R) counters, but that is a different
contract and cannot preserve record identities by value reconstruction alone. Specialized
variants require their own algorithm and proof rather than borrowing the CLRS properties
wholesale.
Coverage audit of this combined corpus
Principles now include contracts, identities, ties, cost models, bounds, invariants, special
domains, semantic interpretation, and method choice. Bubble and selection include complete
explanations, pseudocode, traces, proofs, exact counts, stability variants, implementations, and
answer banks. Insertion adds inversion-sensitive analysis, binary insertion, and hybrids. Merge
adds sentinel-free code, range conventions, peak-space accounting, adaptive variants, and
inversion counting. Counting adds signed domains, stable placement proofs, range queries, and
radix connections.
The 55 retained source pages remain unchanged. A replacement contents page and 44
supplements produce exactly 100 PDF pages. Source references retain printed pagination;
supplements use S-section names and PDF positions.
Remaining boundaries
This focused corpus covers the five requested methods. Brief adjoining topics remain on
preserved whole source pages. The checked teaching code illustrates its stated contracts;
application-specific validation remains separate.
